title: 3. Distribution, Supply Chain & Unit Economics

epigraph.quote: Profitability is decided on the factory floor, but cash flow is decided in the receivables ledger and the spares warehouse.
epigraph.author: Manufacturing Forensics

web_blocks.html: Eimco Elecon builds its machines at a single 15-acre plant in Vallabh Vidyanagar, Anand (Gujarat). A DSIR-approved in-house R&D centre backs the factory. The company also runs 10 regional sales and service offices with parts depots across India's mining and infrastructure hubs. Those hubs cover Asansol, Bilaspur, Dhanbad, Kolkata, Nagpur, Secunderabad, Bengaluru, Chennai, Jamshedpur, Mumbai, and New Delhi. Crucially, Eimco Elecon uses a related party, Emtici Marketing LLP, to win mining orders and coordinate field support. It pays Emtici a sales-linked commission. That related-party distribution setup warrants ongoing governance checks.

On the supply side, Eimco Elecon has achieved high local content in steel fabrication, assemblies, and its Continuous Miner package. Still, key hydraulic, electronic, and powertrain parts carry long import lead times. Those imports include Hitachi base platforms for piling rigs and specialized flameproof battery parts. PSU clients also expect critical spares to sit ready across all 10 regional depots. As a result, Eimco Elecon holds ~211–270 days of inventory (CRISIL Aug 2026: ~211 days in FY26 vs. ~216 days in FY25). On the customer side, PSU tenders from CIL, SCCL, and UCIL include milestone acceptance and retention rules. Those terms kept receivables at ~115 days in FY26, up from 101 days in FY25 but below the 150–178 days seen earlier. Private MDOs and contractors grew to roughly 50% of sales in FY26. That shift gives management a chance to cut debtor days, even though private orders bring delivery deferrals.

The FY2026 unit-economics waterfall above comes from audited FY26 BSE/NSE filings and the 52nd Annual Report. Measured per ₹100 of revenue, it highlights two core truths. First, core operating profitability is genuinely healthy. Gross margin stands at ~42.1%, while employee costs take 9.5% of sales (₹22.01 Cr). Other operating expenses—covering R&D, marketing, and related-party commissions—take 14.0% (₹32.32 Cr). That leaves an 18.6% operating EBITDA margin (₹42.8–43.0 Cr) and a 14.7% EBIT margin. FY26 normalized from FY25's peak 22.8% EBITDA margin, which included a one-time high-margin order.

Second, weak cash conversion and treasury income heavily shape the bottom line. In FY26, Other Income reached ₹17.05 Cr (7.4% of sales) from ~₹206 Cr of mutual fund and treasury holdings. That boost lifted PBT to ₹50.36 Cr and PAT to ₹38.71 Cr (16.8% net margin). However, Cash Flow from Operations (CFO) was only ₹22.10 Cr (9.6% of sales, or ~51% of EBITDA) because working capital absorbed cash. At the same time, Eimco Elecon spent ₹60.50 Cr on capex (26.2% of sales), covering Kanjari land and plant upgrades. That capex pushed Free Cash Flow to -₹38.40 Cr in FY26, compared with +₹27.20 Cr in FY25. In H1 FY27, Net PPE rose further to ₹112 Cr (from ₹64 Cr in March 2026). Meanwhile, H1 FY27 CFO was just ₹2 Cr as working capital absorbed ₹16 Cr.

Coal India Tender Mechanics & The Working-Capital Lockup: A debt-free OEM with ~42% gross margins still holds ~211 days of inventory and ~115 days of receivables. To see why, trace how Indian PSU mining tenders work. Coal India subsidiaries (SECL, MCL, WCL, ECL, BCCL) and SCCL award contracts via competitive e-tendering. Those tenders enforce strict technical rules, multi-stage inspections, and bank guarantees. Payments follow milestones: a major tranche arrives after dispatch and underground commissioning, while retention money (often 10%) waits for trial availability sign-offs. Continuous Miners and piling rigs also need imported hydraulic pumps, flameproof electrical modules, and Hitachi base platforms with multi-month lead times. Management must order those parts well before tenders close. When a PSU buyer or private MDO delays delivery by even one quarter—as in FY26—finished machines sit on the books, bloating working capital and lowering cash conversion.

Indigenization Economics & The Emtici Marketing Distribution Structure: Inside the plant, Eimco Elecon's DSIR-approved R&D centre has steadily raised domestic content. Its 100% homegrown Continuous Miner package avoids the import duties and assembly cost penalties that foreign rivals face. That local engineering supports steady 18–20% operating EBITDA margins even when raw material costs hover near 57.9% of sales. On the sales side, Eimco Elecon relies on promoter-group firm Emtici Marketing LLP for mining outreach and field coordination. Emtici earns sales-linked commissions, which sit inside FY26's ₹32.32 Cr of other operating expenses. Emtici's coalfield ties help defend Eimco's 65–70% intermediate-loader share. Even so, minority shareholders must watch these related-party commissions closely as private MDOs reach ~50% of sales.

Working-Capital Sensitivity & Fixed-Cost Absorption: Eimco Elecon pairs modest fixed employee costs (₹22.01 Cr in FY26, or 9.5% of sales) with flexible subcontracting and bought-out parts (57.9% COGS). Operating leverage kicks in cleanly once quarterly sales pass ₹60–75 Cr, lifting operating margins toward 20%. During slowdowns, high-margin spares help cushion the margin drop. The real bottleneck is capital velocity. Holding 211 days of inventory—depot spares plus long-lead imported hydraulics and Hitachi platforms—and 115 days of receivables ties up heavy cash. Every ₹100 Cr of new annual sales requires roughly ₹55–65 Cr of added net working capital unless payment terms tighten.

web_blocks.title: Unit-Economics Takeaway: High Gross/EBITDA Margin, Heavy Working-Capital Tax
paragraphs: Eimco Elecon earns ~18.5–20% EBITDA margins on its engineering, which is solid for Indian capital goods. Yet every ₹100 of added revenue typically ties up ₹55–65 of net working capital (inventory plus receivables minus payables).
Until inventory days (~211) and debtor days (~115) fall structurally, growth will keep absorbing cash before generating it.

book_paragraphs: To understand how a heavy engineering company actually makes money, you and I have to trace ₹100 of revenue from the moment a steel frame is welded at the Vallabh Vidyanagar factory until the cash finally clears in Eimco Elecon's bank account. In FY2026, the company generated ₹230.7 crore in revenue from operations, and the audited income statement reveals a fascinating tension: genuinely strong engineering margins paired with stubbornly slow working-capital velocity.

Let us walk down the ₹100 waterfall together. Out of every ₹100 of sales in FY26, raw materials, steel plates, and bought-out hydraulic and electronic components consumed roughly ₹57.90, leaving a healthy gross margin of ₹42.10. Employee costs for the company's skilled engineers, machinists, and field service technicians took ₹9.54, while other operating expenses—including power, freight, R&D, and sales commissions paid to related-party Emtici Marketing LLP—took ₹14.01. That left an operating EBITDA of ₹18.55 per ₹100 of sales, or ₹43.0 crore in total—right inside management's 18% to 20% steady-state guidance band, even after normalizing from FY25's one-off 22.8% peak.

Below EBITDA, depreciation was modest at ₹3.81 per ₹100 and interest expense was virtually nonexistent at ₹0.29—because Eimco Elecon carries negligible debt and enjoys a 50.51x interest coverage ratio. Then came a major non-operating boost: ₹7.39 per ₹100 of Other Income, or ₹17.05 crore, earned from the company's ₹206 crore treasury portfolio of mutual funds and liquid investments. After ₹5.05 in taxes, net profit landed at ₹16.78 per ₹100, or ₹38.71 crore. On the surface, a 16.8% net margin looks like an effortless cash machine—until you and I turn the page to the cash flow statement.

book_subsections.title: Why Coal India Tenders and Spares Depots Trap Cash
paragraphs: Out of ₹43.0 crore in FY26 EBITDA, only ₹22.1 crore—roughly ₹9.58 per ₹100 of sales, or just over half of operating profit—converted into Cash Flow from Operations. Why did nearly half the operating profit stay trapped outside the bank account? Because Eimco Elecon operates at the intersection of two working-capital-heavy realities. On the supply side, imported hydraulic pumps, flameproof electricals, and Hitachi base platforms for piling rigs carry long lead times, while Coal India and Singareni Collieries expect spare parts to sit ready across 10 regional depots. That forces Eimco Elecon to hold roughly 211 days of inventory.

On the customer side, PSU mining tenders run on milestone-based acceptance, underground commissioning sign-offs, and retention clauses that keep receivables sitting at 115 days. Even though private-sector MDOs now account for roughly 50% of revenue, private contractors can still defer deliveries when mine clearances slip—as happened in H1 FY27, when ₹16 crore was absorbed by working capital and operating cash flow came in at just ₹2 crore despite a 33.3% revenue jump. Add ₹60.5 crore of FY26 capex for Kanjari land and plant expansion, and Free Cash Flow flipped to negative ₹38.4 crore. None of this is reckless—it was funded 100% from internal accruals with zero debt—but it proves that scaling a heavy-equipment OEM consumes cash upfront before it compounds.

book_subsections.title: Inside a Coal India Tender: Why Cash Arrives Months After the Steel Ships
paragraphs: To really feel why Eimco Elecon's cash conversion lags its accounting profits, you and I have to follow a Coal India or Singareni Collieries tender from start to finish. It begins months before a single rupee of revenue is booked. Because specialized hydraulic valves, flameproof electrical switchboxes, and Hitachi base platforms for piling rigs carry long import lead times, Eimco Elecon has to commit capital to raw materials and sub-assemblies well in advance. Meanwhile, its 10 regional depots must stay stocked with slow-moving but mission-critical spares so PSU clients never face downtime.

Once a machine is fabricated and tested in Vallabh Vidyanagar, it is trucked to a coalfield in Chhattisgarh or Jharkhand. Unlike a consumer product where cash changes hands at the store counter, PSU mining contracts release payment in stages: an initial tranche after dispatch and underground commissioning, and a final retention slice—often 10%—only after the machine clears multi-week availability trials underground. If a mine gallery isn't ready, or if a private MDO's environmental clearance slips by two months, finished machines sit in Eimco Elecon's yard while receivables sit at 115 days.

Look at what that did in H1 FY27: revenue jumped 33.3% year-on-year to ₹134.3 crore, and EBITDA hit ₹25 crore, yet Cash Flow from Operations was just ₹2 crore because ₹16 crore went straight into funding inventory and receivables. That is not a sign of poor product demand—quite the opposite—but it teaches us a vital rule for heavy machinery: growth eats cash before it spits cash back out.

book_subsections.title: Why Inventory Days and Receivable Days Are the Real Management Scorecard
paragraphs: If you sit down with a seasoned capital-goods analyst to review Eimco Elecon's annual report, notice where their eyes go first: not to the headline EBITDA margin, which management has reliably kept in the 18% to 20% band, but to two lines on the balance sheet—inventories and trade receivables. At 211 days of inventory and 115 days of receivables in FY26, Eimco Elecon holds roughly nine to ten months of revenue tied up in raw materials, work-in-progress machines, depot spares, and unpaid customer bills.

Why does that matter so much to you and me? Because working capital acts like an invisible tax on growth. When Coal India or a private Mine Developer-cum-Operator awards a ₹50 crore Continuous Miner order, Eimco Elecon must first spend cash on imported hydraulic pumps, flameproof motors, and steel fabrication months before it collects the final retention payment. If management can trim inventory from 211 days toward 160 days through better supply-chain planning and collect faster from private contractors, tens of crores of trapped cash will flow straight back into the bank—dramatically improving cash conversion without selling a single extra machine.

There is one more subtle lesson hidden inside Eimco Elecon’s FY26 unit economics. Notice how employee expenses stood at just ₹22.01 crore—roughly 9.54% of revenue—while raw materials and bought-out components consumed 57.90%. That tells you Eimco Elecon runs a lean core workforce of engineers, machinists, and regional service technicians, using flexible subcontracting and vendor fabrication to absorb volume swings. When quarterly revenue rises above ₹60 crore, fixed employee overhead barely budges, allowing operating margins to expand cleanly toward the 20% mark. Conversely, when tender dispatches pause, that lean payroll keeps the factory profitable instead of bleeding cash.

When you and I check future quarterly results, the single sharpest indicator of improving cash quality will be whether inventory days begin stepping down from 211 days toward the 160-to-170-day range while revenue stays above ₹250 crore annually.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION: The Emtici Marketing Watchpoint
book_callouts.text: Eimco Elecon routes a meaningful share of its mining sales and after-sales coordination through Emtici Marketing LLP, a promoter-group related party, for a percentage commission. You and I should inspect the Related Party Transactions schedule in every annual report to verify that commission rates stay transparent and proportionate as private-sector orders grow.
